title: 〜て・〜で (cause)
meaning: Links a cause and its result with the te-form. The second clause is usually a feeling, an evaluation, or a result nobody can control.
connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective くて / na-adjective or noun + で + result

senses.label: Verb te-form
senses.meaning: The first clause is the cause; the second is the feeling or state it leads to. The second clause is often 「うれしい」, 「びっくりした」, 「すみません」, etc. It sounds natural and soft, and doesn't stress the reason the way 「から」 does.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + feeling / evaluation (〜て、うれしい／〜て、すみません)
examples: I was surprised to hear the news.
I'm happy I was able to pass the exam.
Sorry I'm late.

senses.label: Adjective くて
senses.meaning: A quality or state described by an adjective causes the result. The second clause is often a potential or state expression such as 「できない」 or 「わからない」.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + くて / negative 「〜なくて」
examples: This question is too hard. I don't understand it.
It was so hot I couldn't sleep.

senses.label: Noun / na-adjective + で
senses.meaning: A noun or na-adjective + 「で」 gives the cause. The noun is often an accident, illness, weather, or disaster. The second clause is usually something that happened on its own.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + で (風邪で・地震で・心配で)
examples: I stayed home from school because of a cold.
The trains stopped because of the earthquake.
I'm so worried I can't sleep.

notes: The second clause can't be a volitional expression, command, request, or invitation. ✕「時間がなくて、タクシーに乗りましょう」. Use 「ので／から」 instead.
The second clause is usually non-volitional: emotion adjectives, negative potential verbs, 「すみません」, 「ありがとう」, etc.
「Noun + で」 can also mark a place or means. Check whether the second clause is a “result” to tell them apart.

daily.title: Apologizing for being late
daily.description: When you're late to meet a friend, give the reason, then apologize.
daily.example: Sorry to keep you waiting.

daily.title: Explaining an absence
daily.description: Telling a teacher or family member why you missed school.
daily.example: I had a fever, so I stayed home from school.

daily.title: Getting a present
daily.description: Saying how you feel about a friend's gift.
daily.example: I was really happy to get the present.

work.title: Thanking a client
work.description: Thanking someone for their help in a business email.
work.example: Thank you for your cooperation. It was a great help.

work.title: Reporting a delay
work.description: Telling your boss you were late because of an accident.
work.example: The train was delayed by an accident, so I was late.

etymology: The connecting particle 「て」 is generally thought to come from the continuative form of the old perfective auxiliary 「つ」. It first showed actions happening one after another. From “A happened, then B” came the natural cause-and-effect reading “B because of A”. 「で」 is the voiced form of 「て」 after ん or voiced sounds; the 「で」 after nouns comes from the copula form 「にて」.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: 「から」 gives a reason subjectively, and the second clause can be a volitional expression, command, or request. 「〜て」 only loosely links cause and result, and its second clause can't be volitional.

similar.title: 〜ので
similar.explanation: 「ので」 explains a cause objectively, and the second clause can be a request (〜ので、待ってください). 「〜て」 can't be used this way.

similar.title: 〜なくて (cause)
similar.explanation: 「なくて」 is the negative of this pattern: “because (something) isn't / doesn't ...”, as in 「お金がなくて、買えない」.

meaning: “Just as ...”: doing something, or something happening, exactly the way it was said, written, thought, or planned.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + とおりに; noun + の + とおりに; noun + どおりに

senses.label: Do as said / shown
senses.meaning: Doing something exactly the way someone said, did, or wrote it: “just as ...”, “the way ...”. Often used with 「言う」, 「教える」, 「書いてある」, and 「見る」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + とおりに (言ったとおりに・書いてあるとおりに)
examples: Please write it just as the teacher said.
I tried doing it the way the manual says.
Please repeat after me slowly, just as I say it.

senses.label: After nouns
senses.meaning: After a noun, it means following what that noun shows. With 「noun + の + とおり」 it is read 「とおり」; directly after a noun it becomes 「どおり」.
senses.connection: Noun + の + とおりに / noun + どおりに (予定どおり・時間どおり・計画通り)
examples: If you follow the map, you'll get to the station.
The train arrived right on time.
Construction is going according to plan.

senses.label: Just as ...
senses.meaning: 「〜とおりだ／〜とおり、」 means things really are as thought or said. Often used to confirm a prediction or agree with someone. 「そのとおりです」 means “Exactly.”
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / noun + とおり、／とおりだ (思ったとおり・予想どおりだ)
examples: Just as I thought, he didn't come.
The result was just as expected.
You're absolutely right.

notes: 「とおり」 is written 「通り」 in kanji, but in this grammar it is often written in kana. Directly after a noun, it is read 「どおり」.
To modify a noun, use 「〜とおりの」: 「思ったとおりの結果」.
「通り」 also means “street” (大通り・この通りは車が多い). That is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Learning to cook
daily.description: A family member reminds you to follow the recipe step by step.
daily.example: If you make it just like the recipe says, it won't fail.

daily.title: Giving a friend directions
daily.description: Telling a friend to follow the map you sent.
daily.example: Come the way the map I sent shows, OK?

daily.title: Agreeing with a friend
daily.description: Your friend is spot on, and you fully agree.
daily.example: Yeah, that's exactly right.

work.title: Updating your boss
work.description: Explaining that a project is on schedule.
work.example: The project is proceeding on schedule.

work.title: Training a new hire
work.description: A senior colleague tells a newcomer to follow the manual.
work.example: Please operate it exactly as written in the manual.

etymology: 「とおり」 is written 「通り」, the noun form of the verb 「通る」 (to pass through). It first meant “a road people pass along”, then “the same route or way of doing things”, which gave the meaning “just as ...”. After a noun, the first sound becomes voiced: 「どおり」.

similar.title: 〜ように (as stated)
similar.explanation: 「〜ように」 is mostly used to introduce an explanation, as in “as mentioned above” or “as you all know”. 「〜とおりに」 stresses doing something exactly like a model, with no difference.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: 「まま」 means leaving something as it is (靴のまま入る). 「とおりに」 means following a model or instruction.

similar.title: 〜に従って
similar.explanation: 「〜に従って」 is more formal and usually follows rules or instructions (ルールに従って). 「とおりに」 is more conversational and can follow verbs like 「言った」 and 「見た」.

meaning: 「〜間」 means something continues throughout a period. 「〜間に」 means something happens at some point within that period.
connection: Verb ている-form / dictionary form, i-adjective, na-adjective + な, noun + の + 間 (に)

senses.label: Throughout the period
senses.meaning: 「〜間」 means the state or action in the second clause continues for the whole period. The second clause often uses 「〜ている」 or 「ずっと」. Like “the whole time ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form / noun + の + 間、(second clause: continuous action or state)
examples: I was in the countryside the whole summer vacation.
While my mother was cooking, I was cleaning my room.
I read a book the whole time I was on the train.

senses.label: At some point within
senses.meaning: 「〜間に」 means a one-time action or change happens at some point before the period ends. Like “while ...” or “during ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form / dictionary form, noun + の + 間に (second clause: one-time action)
examples: A burglar broke in while I was away.
I did the laundry while the kids were asleep.
I want to climb Mt. Fuji while I'm in Japan.

notes: With 「間」, the second clause is a continuing state; with 「間に」, it is a one-time action. ✕「寝ている間、電話が来た」. Say 「寝ている間に」.
「間」 is read 「あいだ」. 「この間」 usually means “the other day”, which is not this grammar point.
「AとBの間」 means “between A and B” in space. That is not this grammar point either.

daily.title: Asking a friend for help
daily.description: Asking a friend to look after your pet while you're away.
daily.example: Could you take care of my cat while I'm on my trip?

daily.title: Doing chores
daily.description: Doing something else while the washing machine runs.
daily.example: I'll go shopping while the washing machine is running.

daily.title: Remembering a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend about your time studying abroad.
daily.example: While I was studying abroad, I kept a diary in Japanese every day.

work.title: Handing over before a vacation
work.description: Asking a coworker to handle things while you're off.
work.example: While I'm on vacation, Tanaka-san will be in charge of this.

work.title: Meeting preparations
work.description: Explaining what should be done during the meeting.
work.example: Please print out the materials while we're in the meeting.

etymology: 「間 (あいだ)」 first meant the gap between two things, that is, “between” in space. It was later used for time, meaning the period between two points. Adding 「に」 places an action at one point within that period.

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: 「うちに」 stresses “while you still can, before things change”, with a feeling that it might be too late later (若いうちに). 「間に」 just states the time span objectively.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: 「ながら」 is one person doing two things at once. With 「間」, the two clauses can have different subjects (母が料理を作っている間、私は掃除した).

similar.title: 〜とき
similar.explanation: 「とき」 refers to a point or period in time without stressing its length. 「間」 stresses the whole span from start to finish.

meaning: Marks a deadline: the action must be done by that time. Like “by ...”.
connection: Noun + までに; verb dictionary form + までに

senses.label: Noun deadline
senses.meaning: After a time noun, it shows a deadline. The second clause is a one-time action that gets completed. Like “by ...”.
senses.connection: Time noun + までに (金曜日までに・5時までに・明日までに)
examples: Please hand in your report by Friday.
I'll be back by five.
Please give me an answer by tomorrow.

senses.label: Verb deadline
senses.meaning: After a verb in dictionary form, it means one thing gets done before something else happens. Often used with 「〜ておく」 for getting ready in advance.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + までに (〜が来るまでに・〜が終わるまでに)
examples: I want to read this book before summer vacation ends.
Let's tidy up the room before he comes.

senses.label: までには
senses.meaning: Adding 「は」 gives 「までには」, which is softer. It means “at least by then”, and often goes with guesses and wishes.
senses.connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + までには (〜と思う／〜たい)
examples: I think I'll be back by evening.
I want to get married by next spring.

notes: 「まで」 means an action continues until a time (5時まで働く). 「までに」 means something is done once before a time (5時までに帰る). Mixing these up is the most common mistake.
「今までに」 and 「これまでに」 mean “so far”, not a deadline.
「参考までに」 is a set phrase meaning “just for reference”.

daily.title: Curfew
daily.description: Parents tell their child what time to be home.
daily.example: Be home by ten.

daily.title: Returning a book
daily.description: A librarian tells someone when a book is due.
daily.example: Please return this book by next Monday.

daily.title: Getting ready for a party
daily.description: Planning with a roommate to be ready before the guests arrive.
daily.example: Let's have the food ready before everyone gets here.

work.title: Giving a task
work.description: A manager tells a staff member the deadline.
work.example: Please put these materials together before tomorrow's meeting.

work.title: Setting a deadline by email
work.description: Asking someone in a business email to reply by a certain date.
work.example: We're sorry to trouble you, but could you reply by the end of this month?

etymology: 「まで」 is generally thought to come from 「真手 (まて)」, a limit you reach. Adding the time particle 「に」 shrinks “up to that limit” into “at some point before the limit”, which gives the deadline meaning.

similar.title: 〜まで (end point)
similar.explanation: 「まで」 is followed by a continuing action: you keep doing it until a time (3時まで寝た). 「までに」 is followed by a one-time action done before a deadline (3時までに起きる).

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: 「まえに」 only shows order (寝る前に歯を磨く). 「までに」 stresses a deadline you must not go past.

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: 「うちに」 means doing something while a state still lasts. 「までに」 takes a clear point in time as the deadline.

title: 〜には (purpose)
meaning: “To do ...”, “If you want to ...”: states a purpose, and the second clause says what is needed or what works best.
connection: Verb dictionary form + には; some suru-nouns + には

senses.label: What it takes
senses.meaning: The first clause gives a purpose; the second says what conditions, money, or time it takes. The second clause is often 「必要だ」, 「〜なければならない」, or 「かかる」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + には、〜が必要だ／〜なければならない／〜がかかる
examples: To get to the station, you need to take a bus.
To get into this university, you have to pass an exam.
Building a house costs a lot of money.

senses.label: Evaluation / recommendation
senses.meaning: The second clause says which method or place is best. It is often 「〜がいい」, 「〜がいちばんだ」, or 「便利だ」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + には、〜がいい／〜がいちばんだ／〜に便利だ
examples: The best way to get good at Japanese is to speak it every day.
This park is a good place for taking photos.

senses.label: After nouns
senses.meaning: Some nouns for actions (合格, 上達, 健康, etc.) can take 「には」 directly. This sounds a bit formal.
senses.connection: Suru-noun + には (合格には・上達には・健康には)
examples: Passing takes daily effort.
Improving takes time.

notes: The second clause explains or evaluates what the purpose needs. It can't be the speaker's own specific action. ✕「駅へ行くには、バスに乗ります」. Use 「ために」 there.
「Noun + には」 often means “for (someone)” (子どもには難しい), which is different. Check whether what comes before is a purpose.
「行くには行ったが」 (“I did go, but ...”) is a concessive use, not this grammar point.

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: A tourist asks a local how to get to a sight.
daily.example: Which bus should I take to get to the temple?

daily.title: Fitness advice
daily.description: A friend wants to lose weight, and you give advice.
daily.example: If you want to lose weight, exercise is the best way.

daily.title: Paperwork
daily.description: A friend asks how to get a membership card.
daily.example: You need ID to get a card.

work.title: Explaining a project
work.description: Explaining in a meeting what the project needs to succeed.
work.example: To make this project a success, we need more staff.

work.title: Job requirements
work.description: A job listing states how to apply.
work.example: To apply, you need to submit a résumé.

etymology: The particle 「に」 marks a goal or destination, and 「は」 makes it the topic. 「〜するには」 literally means “as for the goal of doing ...”, which became “if you want to do ...”.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: After 「ために」, the second clause is an action taken to reach the goal (合格するために勉強する). After 「には」, it is usually a requirement or evaluation (合格するには勉強が必要だ).

similar.title: 〜には (for someone)
similar.explanation: 「Noun + には」 means “for ...” (私には難しい) and shows whose point of view an evaluation comes from. In this grammar point, what comes before is a purpose.

similar.title: 〜のに (use)
similar.explanation: 「のに」 often goes with 「使う・便利だ・必要だ」 and shows what something is used for (料理するのに使う). 「には」 more often goes with 「必要だ・いい」 and feels more like stating a goal.

title: 〜で作る・〜から作る (materials)
meaning: Shows what something is made from. Use 「で」 when you can still see the original material, and 「から」 when you can't.
connection: Noun + で／から + 作る (作られる・できている)

senses.label: で: materials
senses.meaning: You can still see the material in the finished product. Like “made of ...”: a table made of wood, a paper plane.
senses.connection: Material noun + で + (〜を) 作る／作られる
examples: I made this desk out of wood.
I made a box out of a milk carton.
This doll is made of paper.

senses.label: から: raw materials
senses.meaning: The raw material has been processed and changed, so you can't see it in the product. Like “made from ...”: wine from grapes, tofu from soybeans.
senses.connection: Raw material noun + から + 作る／作られる
examples: Wine is made from grapes.
Sake is made from rice.
Tofu is made from soybeans.

senses.label: でできている
senses.meaning: 「〜でできている」 and 「〜からできている」 describe what something consists of. They describe a state. The で / から distinction is the same as above.
senses.connection: Noun + で／から + できている／できた
examples: This house is made of stone.
Water is made up of hydrogen and oxygen.

notes: The rule: if you can see the material in the product, use 「で」; if not, use 「から」. Sometimes either works; the line isn't absolute.
The passive 「〜で／から作られる」 is common when describing what products or local specialties are made from.
In 「台所で作る」 and 「自分で作る」, 「で」 marks a place or a way of doing something, not a material.

daily.title: Arts and crafts
daily.description: A child shows a parent something they made.
daily.example: I made this out of paper cups.

daily.title: Local specialties
daily.description: A tour guide introduces a local product.
daily.example: These sweets are made from local rice.

daily.title: Talking about furniture
daily.description: A friend compliments your table, and you explain what it's made of.
daily.example: I had this table made out of old wood.

work.title: Introducing a product
work.description: Telling a client what a product is made from.
work.example: This product is made from recycled plastic.

work.title: Explaining materials
work.description: A shop clerk tells a customer what a bag is made of.
work.example: This bag is made of genuine leather.

etymology: 「で」 is the particle for means and materials, from the classical 「にて」. 「から」 originally marks a starting point: the raw material is where the change starts on the way to becoming a product. That is why it's used when the original form can't be seen.

similar.title: 〜で (means / method)
similar.explanation: The material 「で」 is a kind of “means” 「で」. A means is a tool (はしで食べる); a material is part of the finished product itself (木で作る).

similar.title: 〜から (starting point)
similar.explanation: 「から」 basically marks a starting point in time or space. For raw materials, think of it as “the starting point of a change”.

similar.title: 〜で (place of action)
similar.explanation: In 「工場で作る」 and 「台所で作る」, 「で」 marks a place. Keep it separate from the material 「で」.

title: 〜と (condition)
meaning: “When A, B (always) happens”: once A is true, B follows naturally and inevitably. Used for natural laws, habits, how machines work, and so on.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form, i-adjective, na-adjective + だ, noun + だ + と

senses.label: Natural result
senses.meaning: Once A happens, B always follows. Used for natural laws, operating machines, giving directions, etc. Like “when / whenever ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + と (〜になると・〜を押すと・まっすぐ行くと)
examples: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
If you press this button, water comes out.
Go straight, and you'll see a bank on the right.

senses.label: Habit / repetition
senses.meaning: Every time someone does A, they do B. Used to describe habits. Like “whenever ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + と、〜 (usually a third person, or your own habit)
examples: My dad turns on the TV as soon as he gets home.
I drink coffee as soon as I get up in the morning.

senses.label: Discovery
senses.meaning: 「〜と、〜た」 means that after doing A, you found B. The second clause is in the past and is often something unexpected.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + と、〜た (窓を開けると、〜ていた)
examples: When I opened the window, it was snowing.
When I got home, my mother was there.

notes: The second clause can't be a volitional expression, wish, command, or request. ✕「駅に着くと、電話してください」. Say 「着いたら」.
Only the dictionary form or nai-form comes before 「と」, never the ta-form.
The 「と」 in 「〜と思う」 and 「〜と言う」 is for quoting, and the 「と」 in 「友達と」 means “with”. Neither is a condition.

daily.title: Giving directions
daily.description: A local explains the way to a tourist.
daily.example: Turn right at the second corner, and you'll see the station.

daily.title: Explaining an appliance
daily.description: Showing a family member how to use a new rice cooker.
daily.example: Just press this button and it cooks the rice.

daily.title: Talking about yourself
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about your habits.
daily.example: Whenever I drink, my face turns red right away.

work.title: Instruction manual
work.description: A manual describes what happens when you operate a device.
work.example: When you turn on the power, the lamp lights up.

work.title: Reporting a trend
work.description: Explaining a market pattern in a report.
work.example: When temperatures rise, drink sales go up.

etymology: Conditional 「と」 is generally thought to have developed from the 「と」 used for listing and quoting, and it became common from the early modern period. It ties two events tightly together, so it means “once A happens, B follows”.

similar.title: 〜ば (hypothetical)
similar.explanation: 「ば」 focuses on the condition itself (“as long as ...”), and the second clause can be a volitional expression or wish. 「と」 focuses on the inevitable result, and its second clause can't be volitional.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 has the widest range: the second clause can be a request or volitional expression. 「と」 is only for natural results, habits, and discoveries.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「なら」 picks up what the other person said and gives advice (京都へ行くなら、新幹線がいい). It doesn't express an inevitable result.

similar.title: 〜たら〜た・〜と〜た (discovery)
similar.explanation: For “discovering” something, both 「と」 and 「たら」 work. 「と」 is a bit more literary and is common in narration in novels.

meaning: “In case ...”, “If ...”: imagines a situation and says what to do if it happens. Common in rules, notices, and instructions.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form / nai-form, i-adjective, na-adjective + な, noun + の + 場合 (は)

senses.label: Hypothetical case
senses.meaning: Imagines a situation, and the second clause gives what to do or the rule. Common in notices, manuals, and rules. More formal than 「〜たら」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form / nai-form, noun + の + 場合は (雨の場合は・遅れる場合は)
examples: In case of rain, the game will be canceled.
If you're going to be late, be sure to let us know.
In case of fire, do not use the elevators.

senses.label: As for someone
senses.meaning: 「Noun + の場合 (は)」 can also mean “in the case of ...”, picking out a specific person or thing.
senses.connection: Noun + の + 場合 (は)、〜 (私の場合は・子どもの場合)
examples: In my case, I commute by train every morning.
For children, the fee is half price.

notes: 「場合」 is for hypothetical cases, not for a one-time event that already happened. ✕「昨日雨が降った場合は」.
It's more formal than 「〜とき」 and common in notices, contracts, and manuals.
「場合によっては」 means “depending on the situation”, and 「〜場合が多い」 means “in many cases”. These are different.

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Agreeing in advance what to do if it rains.
daily.example: If it rains, shall we go to a movie?

daily.title: Station announcement
daily.description: A sign at a station informs passengers.
daily.example: If you have left something behind, please tell a station attendant.

work.title: Leave rules
work.description: Company rules explain how to take a day off.
work.example: If you will be absent, contact your manager before work starts.

work.title: Contract terms
work.description: A contract states what happens if a term is broken.
work.example: If payment is not made by the deadline, the contract will be terminated.

work.title: Customer service
work.description: A customer service rep explains the return policy.
work.example: If there is a defect in the product, we will exchange it.

etymology: 「場合」 is made of 「場」 (place) and 「合い」 (meeting). It first meant “the place where a situation comes up”, that is, “occasion, case”. With 「は」 as the topic marker, it introduces a hypothetical case.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 is conversational and very versatile. 「場合は」 is more formal, common in rules and explanations, and usually refers to situations that could happen again.

similar.title: 〜とき
similar.explanation: 「とき」 can refer to a time that actually happened (昨日帰ったとき). 「場合」 is only for hypothetical cases, not specific past events.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「なら」 usually picks up something the other person mentioned and gives advice. 「場合は」 objectively sets up a situation and then explains how to handle it.

meaning: “You just need to ...”, “All you have to do is ...”: gives advice or a method. As a question, it asks “What should I do?” It can also express a wish.
connection: Verb / adjective ba-form + いい (書けばいい・安ければいい)

senses.label: Advice / method
senses.meaning: Tells someone how to reach their goal: “just do this and it's fine”. It sounds relaxed, sometimes with a hint of “it's easy”.
senses.connection: Verb ba-form + いい (〜ばいいです／〜ばいいよ)
examples: If you don't understand, just ask the teacher.
You just need to take this medicine three times a day.
You can just take the bus to the station.

senses.label: Asking what to do
senses.meaning: With a question word, it asks what you should do: “What should I ...?” Common when asking for advice or help.
senses.connection: Question word + verb ba-form + いいですか／いいでしょうか
examples: What should I do?
What should I bring?

senses.label: Wish
senses.meaning: 「〜ばいいなあ」 hopes something will come true. 「〜ばいいのに」 shows dissatisfaction with how things are and wishes they were different, with a sense of regret.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective ba-form + いいなあ／いいのに
examples: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.
I wish I lived closer to the station.

notes: 「〜ばいい」 and 「〜たらいい」 are mostly interchangeable. 「〜ばいい」 focuses on the condition itself, with a feeling of “that's all it takes”.
In writing, 「〜ばよい」 is common.
When said about someone else, 「〜ばいいのに」 can sound critical (言えばいいのに = “You could have just said so”).

daily.title: Giving a friend an idea
daily.description: A friend doesn't know how to contact a teacher, so you make a suggestion.
daily.example: Why don't you just send an email?

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Asking station staff where to change trains.
daily.example: Where should I change trains to get to Shinjuku?

daily.title: Looking forward to the weekend
daily.description: Talking with family about a weekend outing.
daily.example: I hope the weather's nice on Sunday.

work.title: Asking a senior colleague
work.description: A new employee checks how to do a task.
work.example: Who should I submit these documents to?

work.title: Explaining how to submit
work.description: Telling a client that submitting documents is easy.
work.example: You can just send us the documents by email.

etymology: Made of the conditional 「ば」 and the adjective 「いい (良い)」: literally “it's good if ...”. From “it's fine once the condition is met” came the uses for advice, asking what to do, and wishes.

similar.title: 〜たらいい
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning; 「たらいい」 is more conversational. When asking what to do, both 「どうしたらいい」 and 「どうすればいい」 are very common.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: 「ほうがいい」 is clear, firm advice after comparing options. 「ばいい」 just points out one way that works.

similar.title: 〜ばよかった
similar.explanation: 「ばよかった」 is past tense and expresses regret about something you didn't do. 「ばいい」 is about now and the future.

meaning: “It would be good to ...”: gives advice. As a question, it asks “What should I do?” It can also express a hope.
connection: Verb / adjective ta-form + らいい (行ったらいい・休んだらいい)

senses.label: Advice
senses.meaning: Suggests that doing something would be a good idea. It sounds gentle, softer than 「〜ほうがいい」. Often 「〜たらいいよ」 or 「〜たらいいと思う」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らいい (よ)／らいいと思う
examples: If you're tired, you should take a little rest.
I think you should talk to the teacher about it.

senses.label: Asking what to do
senses.meaning: With a question word, it asks what you should do. One of the most common ways to ask for help in daily life.
senses.connection: Question word + verb ta-form + らいいですか／らいいでしょうか
examples: What should I do?
Where should I submit this document?

senses.label: Hope
senses.meaning: 「〜たらいいなあ」 hopes something will happen. 「〜たらいいのに」 wishes for something contrary to reality, with a sense of regret.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective ta-form + らいいなあ／らいいのに
examples: I hope the weather's good tomorrow.
I wish summer vacation would hurry up and come.

notes: 「〜たらいい」 and 「〜ばいい」 are interchangeable in most cases. 「たらいい」 is more conversational.
When advising a superior, 「〜たらいい」 can sound too casual. Use 「〜てはいかがでしょうか」 instead.
The question 「どうしたらいいですか」 is the basic pattern for asking someone for advice.

daily.title: A friend can't sleep
daily.description: A friend says they can't sleep, and you give advice.
daily.example: You should try not to look at your phone before bed.

daily.title: Lost and asking for help
daily.description: Asking a passerby for help in an unfamiliar place.
daily.example: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

daily.title: Looking forward to the holidays
daily.description: Chatting with classmates about vacation.
daily.example: I wish every day were Sunday.

work.title: Asking your boss
work.description: Checking with your boss when you're not sure how to proceed.
work.example: How would you like me to proceed with this matter?

work.title: Advising a coworker
work.description: A coworker has a problem, and you casually suggest something.
work.example: I think you should ask Yamada-san in accounting.

etymology: Made of the conditional 「たら」 and 「いい (良い)」: literally “it's good if you do ...”. 「たら」 comes from 「たら」, a form of the old perfective auxiliary 「たり」, plus 「ば」; the 「ば」 was later usually dropped.

similar.title: 〜ばいい
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning. 「ばいい」 focuses on “just meeting the condition is enough”; 「たらいい」 is more conversational and more common in questions.

similar.title: 〜たらどうですか
similar.explanation: 「たらどうですか」 directly urges the listener to do something and is more pushy. 「たらいい」 just offers a suggestion to consider.

similar.title: 〜といい・〜たらいい (hope)
similar.explanation: For hopes, both 「〜といいね」 and 「〜たらいいね」 work. 「といい」 is often used for wishing others well.

meaning: Makes a suggestion to the listener: “Why don't you ...?”, “How about ...?”
connection: Verb ta-form + らどうですか (らどう？・らいかがですか)

senses.label: General suggestion
senses.meaning: Actively encourages the listener to do something: “Why don't you ...?” In speech, it's often shortened to 「〜たらどう？」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らどうですか／らどう？ (〜てみたらどう)
examples: Why don't you take a little break?
Why don't you go see a doctor?
Why don't you try asking him directly?

senses.label: Polite suggestion
senses.meaning: 「〜たらいかがですか」 replaces 「どう」 with the more polite 「いかが」. Used with guests, older people, or in customer service.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らいかがですか／らいかがでしょうか
examples: Why don't you take this seat?
Why not give it a try?

senses.label: Annoyance / criticism
senses.meaning: 「〜たらどうなの」 and 「〜たらどうだ」 sound annoyed or pushy: “Why don't you just ...!” Only used with people close to you or people below you.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らどうなの／らどうだ
examples: Stop complaining and do it yourself, why don't you.
You could at least help a little.

notes: 「〜たらどうですか」 can sound rude to older people or superiors. In formal situations, use 「〜てはいかがでしょうか」.
「〜たらどうなる？」 asks about a result (“What happens if ...?”), and 「〜たらどうしよう」 expresses worry. Neither is a suggestion.
It's not used for the speaker's own actions. To invite someone to do something together, use 「〜ませんか」 or 「〜ましょう」.

daily.title: A friend has a cold
daily.description: Your friend keeps coughing, and you urge them to see a doctor.
daily.example: Why don't you hurry up and go to the hospital?

daily.title: A friend can't decide on a gift
daily.description: Your friend doesn't know what to give, so you suggest something.
daily.example: Why don't you give her flowers? I'm sure she'll love them.

daily.title: A parent nagging
daily.description: A mother is annoyed with her child who won't get up.
daily.example: It's already ten. Get up already, will you?

work.title: Making a proposal in a meeting
work.description: Suggesting an improvement to colleagues in a meeting.
work.example: How about making the materials a bit simpler?

work.title: Hosting a client
work.description: Politely suggesting a guest take a rest.
work.example: You must be tired after your long trip. Why don't you rest for a while?

etymology: Made of the conditional 「たら」 and 「どうですか」, which asks for an opinion: literally “How would it be if you did ...?” By asking the listener's opinion, it makes a suggestion indirectly.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: 「ほうがいい」 is clear advice after comparing, sounds strong, and can be a warning. 「たらどうですか」 offers one option and lets the listener decide.

similar.title: 〜たらいい
similar.explanation: 「たらいい」 states “it would be good to do this”. 「たらどうですか」 urges the listener directly in question form.

similar.title: 〜はどうですか・〜はいかがですか
similar.explanation: 「Noun + はどうですか」 recommends a thing or asks for impressions (コーヒーはどうですか). 「たらどうですか」 suggests taking an action.

meaning: Expresses regret: “I should have ...”, “I wish I had ...”. What's described didn't actually happen, or the opposite did.
connection: Verb ba-form + よかった (negative: 〜なければよかった)

senses.label: Regret for not doing
senses.meaning: The speaker regrets not doing something. Reality is the opposite of what's said. Like “I should have ...”. Often ends with 「〜なあ」.
senses.connection: Verb ba-form + よかった (なあ)
examples: I should have studied more.
I should have brought an umbrella.

senses.label: Regret for doing
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜なければよかった」 regrets doing something: “I shouldn't have ...”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なければよかった
examples: I shouldn't have said that.
I shouldn't have eaten so much.

senses.label: Regret about others
senses.meaning: 「〜ばよかったのに」, said about someone else, shows pity or mild criticism: “You should have ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ba-form + よかったのに
examples: You should have told me sooner.
You should have come too.

notes: You can also say 「〜たらよかった」 with the same meaning. It's more conversational.
Said to others, 「〜ばよかったのに」 sounds critical, so be careful using it with superiors.
「〜てよかった」 means “I'm glad that ...” (合格してよかった). It shows relief, the opposite feeling.

daily.title: After an exam
daily.description: Complaining to a friend after doing badly on a test.
daily.example: I should have gone to bed earlier last night.

daily.title: Shopping regret
daily.description: Finding out after buying something that it was cheaper elsewhere.
daily.example: I should have bought it at that other store.

daily.title: A friend missed a party
daily.description: Telling a friend who didn't come that the party was fun.
daily.example: It was fun. You should have come too.

work.title: Reflecting on a mistake
work.description: Reflecting in a meeting after a project ran into trouble.
work.example: I regret that I didn't check more carefully beforehand.

work.title: Warning a staff member
work.description: A manager speaks to someone who didn't report a problem in time.
work.example: If there was a problem, you should have reported it right away.

etymology: Made of the conditional 「ば」 and 「よかった」, the past of 「よい (良い)」: literally “it would have been good if ...”. Because the condition is contrary to fact, it became a set phrase for regret.

similar.title: 〜ばいい
similar.explanation: 「ばいい」 offers a method or wish for now or the future. 「ばよかった」 looks back at the past with regret.

similar.title: 〜てよかった
similar.explanation: 「てよかった」 is relief about something that happened. 「ばよかった」 is regret about something that didn't.

similar.title: 〜ば〜のに
similar.explanation: 「〜ば〜のに」 is broader: a contrary-to-fact supposition with dissatisfaction. 「ばよかったのに」 is its most common fixed form.

meaning: Gives permission or makes a concession: “It's OK to ...”, “I don't mind if ...”. Slightly more formal than 「〜てもいい」.
connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective くて / na-adjective or noun + で + もかまわない (構わない)

senses.label: Permission
senses.meaning: Allows someone to do something, or asks if it's OK to do it. The question 「〜てもかまいませんか」 is a polite way to ask for permission.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もかまわない／もかまいません (か)
examples: Is it all right to take photos here?
You may use this pen.
If you're tired, it's fine to go home first.

senses.label: Concession / don't mind
senses.meaning: After an adjective or noun, it means “I don't mind if it's ...”, stating a condition you can accept.
senses.connection: i-adjective くて / noun, na-adjective + で + もかまわない
examples: I don't mind if the room is small.
Tomorrow is fine for getting in touch.
I don't mind if it's a bit expensive.

senses.label: Don't have to
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜なくてもかまわない」 means it's fine not to do something: “You don't have to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なくてもかまわない
examples: You don't have to come tomorrow.
You don't have to eat all of it.

notes: Close in meaning to 「〜てもいい」, but 「かまわない」 is a bit more formal and also suggests “it doesn't bother me”.
In kanji it's 「構わない」, and the polite form is 「かまいません」.
To grant a request, you can simply say 「ええ、かまいませんよ」.

daily.title: At a friend's house
daily.description: Asking if you can use something at a friend's place.
daily.example: Mind if I use your bathroom?

daily.title: Looking for an apartment
daily.description: Telling a real estate agent what you're looking for.
daily.example: I don't mind if it's a bit far from the station.

daily.title: Meeting up
daily.description: A friend says they'll be late, and you say it's fine.
daily.example: It's fine if you're a little late.

work.title: Checking how to submit
work.description: Checking whether you can send something electronically.
work.example: Would it be all right to send the documents by email?

work.title: Job interview
work.description: A candidate says what conditions they can accept.
work.example: I don't mind being posted outside the city.

etymology: 「かまう (構う)」 means “to mind, to care about”. Its negative 「かまわない」 means “not to mind”. 「〜てもかまわない」 literally means “even if ..., I don't mind”, which gives permission and concession.

similar.title: 〜てもいい
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「てもいい」 is more common and conversational; 「てもかまわない」 is a bit more formal and stresses “I don't mind”.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: 「なくてもいい」 and 「なくてもかまわない」 mean the same; the latter is a bit more formal.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: 「ても」 alone just means “even if”. Only with 「かまわない」 does it become a permission expression, “it's OK to ...”.

meaning: Casual contractions of 「なくては」 and 「なければ」 meaning “have to ...”. The 「いけない」 after them is often dropped.
connection: Verb nai-form + なくちゃ／なきゃ (+ いけない・だめ)

senses.label: Have to (shortened)
senses.meaning: Drops the 「いけない」 and ends the sentence with 「なくちゃ」 or 「なきゃ」. Usually said to yourself or to people close to you, about something you have to do.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なくちゃ／なきゃ。
examples: Oh, look at the time. I've got to go home.
I have to write my report by tomorrow.
I need to go to bed early.

senses.label: Full form
senses.meaning: Followed by 「いけない」 or 「だめ」, it expresses obligation or advice to others. More casual than 「〜なければならない」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なくちゃいけない／なきゃだめ
examples: I have to take my medicine.
You've got to practice every day.

senses.label: Unless ..., not
senses.meaning: As a condition, it means “if you don't do A, B won't happen”. The second clause is usually negative.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なきゃ／なくちゃ + negative result
examples: If we don't hurry, we won't make it.
You can't tell until you actually see it.

notes: 「なくちゃ」 comes from 「なくては」, and 「なきゃ」 comes from 「なければ」.
These are spoken forms. Don't use them in formal writing or formal situations with superiors; use 「〜なければなりません」 then.
「なきゃ」 is even more casual than 「なくちゃ」 and is popular with young people.

daily.title: Before leaving in the morning
daily.description: Muttering to yourself when you see how late it is.
daily.example: Oh no, I have to leave now.

daily.title: Reminding a friend
daily.description: Your friend has a test tomorrow but is still playing.
daily.example: You've got a test tomorrow, right? You need to study.

daily.title: Weekend plans
daily.description: Telling your family what you need to do this weekend.
daily.example: I've got to clean my room this weekend.

work.title: Chatting with a coworker
work.description: Telling a coworker you're close to what you still need to do.
work.example: I still have to make the materials for this afternoon's meeting.

work.title: Before leaving work
work.description: Telling a coworker you can't leave yet.
work.example: I just need to answer this email. You can go ahead.

etymology: 「なくちゃ」 is a sound change from 「なくては」: 「ては」 → 「ちゃ」. 「なきゃ」 comes from 「なければ」: 「ければ」 → 「けりゃ」 → 「きゃ」. Both are contractions that formed in speech to say things faster.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: The original form. It's more formal and can be used in writing and formal situations. 「なきゃ／なくちゃ」 are its spoken contractions.

similar.title: 〜ないといけない
similar.explanation: Also very common in speech, with a similar meaning. It can be shortened to end with 「〜ないと」 (もう行かないと).

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: 「ちゃいけない」 (contraction of 「ては」) is a prohibition: “you must not”. 「なくちゃいけない」 is an obligation: “you must”. They mean the opposite.

title: 〜ることがある (sometimes)
meaning: Something doesn't always happen, but happens now and then: “sometimes ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form, i-adjective + ことがある

senses.label: Sometimes do
senses.meaning: Says someone sometimes does something, or something sometimes happens, but not often. Often used with 「ときどき」 or 「たまに」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことがある／ことがあります
examples: I sometimes walk to work.
This train is sometimes late in the morning.
Once in a while I go to the movies alone.

senses.label: Sometimes don't
senses.meaning: After the nai-form, it means “sometimes doesn't ...”: usually it happens, but there are exceptions.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ことがある
examples: When I'm busy, I sometimes skip lunch.
He sometimes doesn't reply to emails.

senses.label: Adjectives
senses.meaning: After an i-adjective, it means a state sometimes occurs. Often used for weather, health, and so on.
senses.connection: i-adjective + ことがある
examples: Around here, it can be cool even in summer.
In spring, it sometimes turns cold suddenly.

notes: Don't confuse this with 「〜たことがある」 (have done before). With the dictionary form, it means “sometimes”; with the ta-form, it's about experience.
「〜こともある」 sounds lighter: “there are also times when ...”.
In 「話したいことがある」 and 「やることがある」 (“I have something to tell you / to do”), 「こと」 is a real noun. That's not this grammar point.

daily.title: Talking about your habits
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about your eating habits.
daily.example: On my days off, I sometimes skip breakfast.

daily.title: Warning a tourist
daily.description: A local warns a tourist about the weather.
daily.example: The weather in the mountains can change suddenly.

work.title: Explaining a system
work.description: Telling a customer what can happen with the system.
work.example: When there's heavy traffic, it can sometimes be hard to connect.

work.title: Explaining work conditions
work.description: In an interview, explaining that overtime or weekend work may come up.
work.example: During busy periods, you may sometimes need to work on Saturdays.

etymology: The formal noun 「こと」 means “matter, situation”, and 「ある」 means “exist”. 「〜ることがある」 literally means “there exist situations where ...”, so it came to mean “sometimes happens”. With the ta-form, it means “there exists such an experience”, the experience use.

similar.title: 〜たことがある
similar.explanation: With the ta-form, it's past experience (日本へ行ったことがある). With the dictionary form, it means something sometimes happens (日本へ行くことがある).

similar.title: 〜こともある
similar.explanation: 「も」 makes it softer and hints “it's not usual, but it does happen”.

similar.title: ときどき〜する
similar.explanation: The adverb 「ときどき」 directly states frequency. 「ことがある」 is less frequent and stresses “occasionally, not always”.
